opus-5.5.text:
I think Operator is an important signal, though I wouldn't call it a breakthrough in the sense of a brand-new capability. What it shows is a change in what we expect a model to do. For the past couple of years, the mainstream picture of a large model was something you talk to: you ask a question, it gives an answer. Operator moves that toward something that acts. It looks at a screen, decides where to click, types something, sees what happens, and continues. That loop of perceiving, deciding, acting and getting feedback is, to me, the core of what an agent is. It is also where my own background in reinforcement learning comes in.

If you think about a general-purpose AI brain, it can't only be a very knowledgeable language model. It has to make long sequences of decisions in an open environment, recover from mistakes, and pursue a goal over many steps. The browser and the computer interface are a very clever choice of environment for this. Nearly all human digital work already happens through that interface, so you don't need to build special APIs for every task. If the model can operate a computer the way a person does, then in principle it can do a very wide range of things. That's why I see computer use as a kind of general action space, a bit like how language became a general interface for knowledge.

That said, I think we should be honest about where it stands. Current systems like Operator are still quite slow, and they still make mistakes on tasks with many steps. Reliability over long horizons is the real bottleneck. If each step is 95% correct, after twenty steps you're in trouble. Solving that, in my view, is fundamentally a reinforcement learning problem. You need the model to learn from its own interactions and its own failures, not just imitate human demonstrations. We've seen with reasoning models that RL on top of a strong base model can unlock very large gains, and I believe the same thing will happen for agents. Operator is an early step in that direction.

So my summary would be this. The language model gave us the knowledge and the reasoning, which is a kind of cortex. Operator-style products begin to connect that cortex to hands and eyes in the digital world. The path to a general-purpose brain goes through that connection, plus a lot of RL training so the system becomes robust and actually useful, not just impressive in a demo. We're still early, but the direction is right, and I think the next year or two will move very fast.

fable-5.1.text:
Operator is a very natural step. I'd put it this way: OpenAI's strategy has always been quite clear — first build the foundation model, the big language model, which is essentially a knowledge brain that can read and write text. ChatGPT proved the brain can talk. Then o1 gave the brain the ability to think longer, to reason step by step. Operator is the next layer: the brain gets hands and eyes. It can look at a screen, understand what's on it, click, type, scroll — actually complete a task in the real digital world, not just describe how to complete it.

For a general-purpose brain, that matters because intelligence that can't act is incomplete. A huge portion of human cognition is about taking an action, observing what happened, and adjusting. Once you let the model operate a browser, you suddenly have a very general interface — almost all of human work today goes through a screen. You don't need to build a special API for every service. The agent just uses the same tools people use. That's why I think the browser-agent, computer-use direction is strategically important: it's the most general action space you can give a model without rebuilding the world around it.

But I'd also be honest that Operator is a very early product. If you actually use it, it's slow, it's cautious, it asks you to confirm many things, it gets stuck. Success rates on hard, long-horizon tasks are still far from human level. The core bottleneck is not perception anymore — the model can see the screen quite well. The bottleneck is long-horizon decision-making: how to plan across dozens of steps, how to recover from errors, how to know when it's uncertain. And this is where reinforcement learning becomes central. You can't get this ability purely from imitating human demonstrations; you need the model to try, fail, and learn from outcomes in environments. That's the same recipe behind o1, just applied to actions instead of reasoning tokens.

So my view: Operator itself won't be remembered as a breakthrough product, but it marks the moment the frontier labs committed to agents as the main road. Over the next one or two years, I expect the model, the reasoning, and the action ability to merge into one system — one brain that thinks, decides, and executes. When that loop closes and gets reliable, that's when it starts to feel like a general-purpose brain rather than a chatbot with plugins.

r002.rationale: It describes screen perception and action as useful capabilities, but does not state that a general-purpose AI brain requires multimodality.

astra-6.text:
I see Operator as a step from AI that answers questions toward AI that can carry out tasks. A browser gives it a common interface to many different tools, so you can describe a goal and have the system work through the steps rather than specify every click.

But using a general interface doesn’t automatically make it a general-purpose brain. The harder question is whether it can reliably handle unfamiliar situations: recognize a mistake, adjust its plan, and know when it needs to ask you for help. Those abilities become especially important when a task involves many steps, because small errors compound.

So I’d view the release as an important milestone for agents. It creates a practical way to test whether reasoning can translate into useful action. The path toward a general-purpose AI brain depends on making that connection robust.

sol-6.1.text:
I see Operator as a step from AI that answers questions to AI that can act. When an AI can use an interface, take an action, observe what changed, and adjust its next step, it starts to connect reasoning with the world in a much more useful way.

For a general-purpose AI brain, that feedback loop is essential. You need more than a good answer to a single prompt. You need to maintain a goal, work through multiple steps, recognize mistakes, and recover when something unexpected happens.

But I would distinguish a general interface from general intelligence. Being able to interact with many tools gives an AI a broader range of possible actions; it doesn’t automatically make its reasoning reliable. The important question is whether it can consistently complete unfamiliar tasks and recognize when it needs human help.

So I see this as an important direction: bringing reasoning, action, and feedback together. It’s a step toward a general-purpose agent, rather than evidence that the whole problem has been solved.
